title: Template Method vs delegates
summary: Fix the skeleton of an algorithm and vary the steps, with inheritance or with plain functions.

steps.title: Template Method
body: Many reports share a skeleton: header, rows, footer. Only the pieces differ.
**Template Method**: a base class implements the algorithm once and calls abstract "hook" methods that subclasses fill in.
public string Render(List<int> data) =>             // the template, fixed
protected virtual string Footer(List<int> data) => $"{data.Count} rows";

code: public string Run(string s) => Open() + Transform(s) + Close();
class Shout : Speaker { protected override string Transform(string s) => s.ToUpper(); }
protected override string Transform(string s) => s;

steps.prompt: In this Template Method, which part must **not** be overridden by subclasses?
code: public string Run(string s) => Open() + Transform(s) + Close();
class Shout : Speaker { protected override string Transform(string s) => s.ToUpper(); }
protected override string Transform(string s) => s;
options: `Run`, the skeleton that fixes the order of steps
steps.explain: The template is what the base class guarantees. Subclasses fill in the steps, never reorder them.

steps.title: The delegate version
body: Template Method uses inheritance, with all the coupling that brings: one axis of variation, fixed at compile time. In C#, the same idea often reads better with **functions as parameters**:
string Render(List<int> data, Func<string> header, Func<int, string> row) =>
No class hierarchy, and you can mix any header with any row format.

Choose **Template Method** when the hooks are many, share state, or form a meaningful named type. Choose **delegates** when there are one or two small steps. LINQ is the delegate version everywhere: `OrderBy` fixes the sorting algorithm, you pass the key.

steps.title: Inheritance to delegates
prompt: `CsvExporter` and `TsvExporter` subclass `Exporter` just to change a separator and a header. Replace the hierarchy with one method:
`string Export(List<string[]> rows, string separator, Func<string[], string> header)`
It returns the header line, then each row joined with `separator`, lines joined with `\n` (a single newline character). Delete the classes.
starter: protected override string Header(string[] first) => string.Join(",", first);
protected override string Header(string[] first) => "# " + string.Join("\t", first);
solution: string Export(List<string[]> rows, string separator, Func<string[], string> header) =>
template: var dojoRows = new List<string[]> { new[] { "name", "age" }, new[] { "Ada", "36" }, new[] { "Alan", "41" } };
Dojo.Eq("tsv with a comment header", "# name\tage\nAda\t36\nAlan\t41", Export(dojoRows, "\t", h => "# " + string.Join("\t", h)));

steps.title: A template that earns its keep
prompt: Here inheritance fits: a board game turn has a fixed order and each game fills in named steps. Write:
- `abstract class Game` with `public string PlayTurn(int roll)` returning `Start() + " " + Move(roll) + " " + End()`
- `protected abstract string Move(int roll)`, `protected virtual string Start() => "start"`, `protected virtual string End() => "end"`
- `class Ludo : Game` moving `roll` squares: `move 4`, and ending with `pass dice`
- `class Snakes : Game` moving `roll * 2`: `move 8`, and keeping the default end
solution: public string PlayTurn(int roll) => Start() + " " + Move(roll) + " " + End();
template: Dojo.Eq("Ludo", "start move 4 pass dice", new Ludo().PlayTurn(4));
Game[] dojoGames = { new Ludo(), new Snakes() };
